extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science; scientifically literate readers interested in the foundations and limits of scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying principles about what laws of nature mean, the limits of induction, and the proper interpretation and scope of scientific inference. Focus is on epistemic constraints, the interplay of laws and initial conditions, and cosmological/speculative implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of a law of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: A law of nature 'is not a uniformity which must be obeyed by all objects, but merely a uniformity which is as a matter of fact obeyed by those objects which have come beneath our observation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When stating a law one ought to join an estimate of the number of instances in which it has been observed to hold true and the probability thence calculated that it will hold true in the next case. Laws are descriptions of observed uniformities, not metaphysical necessities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive inference is always fallible
rubrics_metrics.description: No finite number of instances can warrant us in expecting with certainty that the next instance will be of like nature; inverse probability formulas include a unit representing the probability that our inference will be mistaken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat inductive conclusions as probabilistic and conditional. Do not claim absolute certainty from finite observation; explicitly account for the residual probability of error when drawing generalisations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance for conceivable exceptions and alternative laws
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not a reproach to scientific method if something were ultimately discovered to possess properties seemingly inconsistent with an established law (e.g., gravity without inertia); fundamental laws (Indestructibility of Matter, Conservation of Energy, Laws of Motion) are not shown to be necessary truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remain open to the conceivability and investigation of other laws; historical examples (Airy, Laplace, Newton) show scientists have explored alternative theoretical laws and their mathematical consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law alone does not determine outcomes (law plus agents)
rubrics_metrics.description: A law by itself determines nothing; it is law plus agents obeying law which has results, and it is no function of law to govern or define the number and place of its own agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When predicting outcomes, account for the distribution, number, and placement (collocation) of particles/agents. The same law with different initial collocations yields different phenomena; therefore analyses must include collocation/initial-condition considerations (Chalmers cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy of laws and possibility of overriding interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: One force may override another, and two laws may each be obeyed and may each disguise the action of the other; there is nothing in science to warrant assigning a limit to this hierarchy of laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect and look for layered/ emergent laws (e.g., magnetic vs gravitational effects, biological 'laws' superadded to physics). Be cautious attributing completeness to any single-level description; search for hidden forces or higher-level regularities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity of 'Uniformity of Nature' — does not preclude catastrophes or discontinuities
rubrics_metrics.description: The Uniformity of Nature, understood as observed laws, does not imply that extensive alterations or sudden catastrophes are impossible; the reign of law is consistent with dramatic, unexpected events and even discontinuities of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate observed regularities with metaphysical guarantees of permanence. Consider long-term astronomical and geological possibilities (comet impacts, planetary disturbances, discontinuities) when evaluating claims about stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive power limited by incomplete data and unknown agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific prediction extends at most to the limits of the data employed; every conclusion is hypothetical and conditional upon the non-interference of agencies previously undetected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess predictions by the completeness of the data and the possibility of undetected agents or causes. Explicitly state assumptions about what is known and what agencies are presumed absent when making forecasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution in extrapolation beyond the domain of data
rubrics_metrics.description: We can seldom trust our best-established theories far from their data; scientific statements and theoretical deductions lose reliability when carried beyond the domain in which they were tested (e.g., thermodynamic extrapolations to infinite past/future).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit inferences to ranges justified by empirical evidence; where extrapolation is necessary, qualify conclusions and acknowledge speculative character. Use known-data boundaries as an explicit constraint on theoretical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require quantitative statement of observational basis and probability
rubrics_metrics.description: With the statement of every law we ought properly to join an estimate of the number of instances in which it has been observed to hold true, and the probability thence calculated that it will hold true in the next case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whenever formulating or evaluating a law, supply (or demand) the empirical base and a probabilistic estimate. Use probabilistic/inverse methods to characterise confidence rather than rhetoric of certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple cosmological states consistent with the same laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The universe might exist consistently with the same laws in the most diverse conditions (e.g., glowing nebula, cooling toward cold solid state); law is not inconsistent with extreme diversity and different global states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that the same underlying laws can yield radically different macroscopic universes depending on initial conditions and large-scale parameters; avoid assuming a single inevitable cosmological trajectory derived solely from law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation and foundational physical laws may be incomplete
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical principles like conservation of energy are strong but not shown to be necessarily exhaustive; foreknowledge of unknown forms of energy or phenomena (neither kinetic nor potential) remains possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remain open to revision of foundational conservation claims in light of new empirical evidence or theoretical insights; avoid dogmatic adherence to current formulations when confronting anomalous phenomena or speculative possibilities (e.g., unknown energies).
